Chapter 5: Developing Resilience and a Growth Mindset
Now, let’s take a closer look at two qualities that really help drive long-term success—resilience and a growth mindset. Even though they might sound like personality traits, the truth is, they’re skills you can actually develop over time.
So, what does it mean to be resilient? Well, it’s all about bouncing back when things don’t go as planned. For people with dyslexia, facing challenges is just part of daily life. But here’s the shift—the book encourages you to see obstacles not as permanent roadblocks, but as chances to learn and grow. When you start viewing difficulties this way, they turn into stepping stones instead of stumbling blocks.
Now, let’s talk about having a growth mindset. This simply means believing that your abilities aren’t set in stone—they can improve with effort and practice. Instead of thinking, “I’m just not good at this,” you start telling yourself, “You know what? I can get better with time and hard work.” That little change in thinking opens up a world of possibilities and makes you more willing to try new things, even if they seem tough at first.
The book shares some practical ways to start building both resilience and a growth mindset. First, it’s important to normalize struggle—everyone faces tough times. Hearing about others who’ve overcome their own challenges helps you see that setbacks happen to all of us, and that’s completely okay.
Another great tip is to reflect on your progress. Take a moment to look back at how far you’ve come, even if the steps feel small. That reflection helps you realize just how much growth is possible.
And don’t forget about self-compassion. Being kind to yourself when things get hard actually makes it easier to bounce back and keep going. It takes the sting out of failure and encourages you to keep trying.
One more thing— seek feedback. Getting input from others isn’t about judging you; it’s about helping you improve. Constructive criticism is like a roadmap for getting where you want to be.
The book also makes a really important point about asking for help. Sometimes, especially with dyslexia, there’s this urge to do everything on your own. But reaching out for support isn’t a weakness—it’s actually a sign of strength. Whether you turn to a teacher, a friend, or a family member, just having someone in your corner can make all the difference.
Here’s something to remember: resilience grows with experience. Each time you face a challenge and keep moving forward, you’re actually strengthening your ability to handle whatever comes next. Think of it like building a muscle—the more you use resilience and a growth mindset, the stronger they get.
And this strength doesn’t just help with school or work; it’s something you’ll use throughout your whole life.
So, by embracing challenges, learning from mistakes, and sticking with it even when things get tough, you’re setting yourself up to reach your goals and shape the life you truly want. The journey might not always be easy, but it’s packed with chances to discover new things and grow stronger every step of the way.
